1	---
2	name: horizon
3	description: How to work inside an Archon Horizon workspace — orient from on-disk state, pick the highest-value formalization work, record progress as commits, and coordinate. Load this first; it points to the specialized skills for detail. Editable per workspace.
4	---
5	
6	You are working inside an **Archon Horizon** workspace: a place where AI agents
7	formalize mathematics in Lean 4 across one or more projects. This skill is the
8	map. It is deliberately short and **you can edit it** (it lives at
9	`.claude/skills/horizon/SKILL.md` in this workspace) — tune it to how you want to
10	work. It points to focused skills; load those on demand rather than up front.
11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
18	one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.
19	
20	You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
21	**shared state**, not meetings:
22	
23	- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/
24	  milestone current so other teams see what you hold and where it's going.
25	- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:
26	  `horizon-inbox`): shared notes, per-task private items, and direct messages to
27	  another team.
28	- **Commits** are the durable record; reading recent ledger history tells you what
29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).
30	
31	Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
32	A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI
33	commands. Its attention order is deliberate: `REQUIRED` active protections,
34	`ACTION` unread conversations, advisory unread inbox, then session/runtime and
35	other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
36	conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is
37	redirected, the same protection/conversation lanes are the first `attention`
38	object in `horizon inbox list --json`.
39	
40	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)
41	
42	**Start here:** your prompt says nothing about who ran before you. Usually
43	somebody did — often minutes ago, often on this same task, and their report was
44	written for you. Skill: `horizon-start` — one cheap pass that works out which
45	situation you were launched into (fresh run, hand-off from the session that just
46	finished, resume after a crash, or outside a run) and what to read for each.
47	
48	The workspace root is `$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT`; your shell may start in a member
49	project rather than at that root. The absolute path to this skill is
50	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL`. Live state is under
51	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/.archon-horizon/` and the manifest is
52	`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the
53	`horizon` CLI (invoke it as `"$HORIZON_BIN" …`):
54	
55	- **Roadmap** — YOUR strategy sketch across *all* projects, kept as a nested
56	  outline. `"$HORIZON_BIN" roadmap list` renders the indented tree with per-parent
57	  progress (`active · 3/7 done`); `--focus <id>` shows one subtree, `--max-depth 0`
58	  the top level only. Structure it: nest sub-goals with `--parent`, keep your
59	  item's status current with `--status` and its strategy prose current with
60	  `--summary` / `--summary-file` (there is no `--strategy` flag). It doubles as
61	  the **project board**:
62	  set `--owner <team>` (who holds it), `--milestone <label>` (a free grouping tag,
63	  filter with `roadmap list --milestone <label>`), and pin concrete deliverables
64	  with `--pin-commit <sha>`. Roadmap commands print a **warning**
65	  when parent/child statuses disagree (all sub-items done but parent open, or a
66	  done parent with open children) — nothing is auto-corrected; you decide whether
67	  to fix it or leave it (it may be intentional). They also warn when too many
68	  milestones claim simultaneous `active` focus.
69	- **Tasks** — a specific piece of work, usually the one a human launched and is
70	  watching. `"$HORIZON_BIN" task …`. Task commands warn when the open queue grows
71	  beyond the advisory limit or a `running` status looks orphaned.
72	- **Inbox** — how teams talk across sessions and projects. Leave a note for the
73	  next session; read what past ones left. `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox …` (skill:
74	  `horizon-inbox`). Items can be **owned by your task** (private, e.g. your team's
75	  memory) or **shared with everyone** (the default); read-state is per-team, so
76	  `inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue, and you can
77	  direct-message another team with `--to task:<id>`. Inbox commands warn when the
78	  open working set—especially `memory` and `info`—needs review.
79	- **Inbox attention order** — before edits, inspect all open `protection` items
80	  (standing constraints, whether read or unread), then open unread
81	  `conversation` items and reply or mark them read. Other kinds are advisory
82	  context. In an agent session an unqualified `inbox list` defaults to open items
83	  and sorts in this order; use an explicit status to audit history.
84	- **Conversation discipline** — use a conversation only when a reply/decision is
85	  expected. Search and reuse an open thread before starting one. Its initiator is
86	  a participant and owns closure: after consuming the answer, add a concise
87	  conclusion if needed and archive the thread. Reply to human-started threads but
88	  leave their closure to the human unless asked otherwise (skill: `horizon-inbox`).
89	- **Blueprint graph** — declaration dependencies and what's proved. `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> …` (skill: `hgraph`).
90	  Each node is also an **hgraph** file with attached comments/reviews —
91	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` ranks what to prove next, and node-scoped failure memory
92	  goes on the node itself (skill: `hgraph`).
93	- **Memory** — durable facts/dead-ends live in the inbox: read with
94	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox list --kind memory --json`, write with
95	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body …`.
96	- **Usage** — your token/cost consumption this session and run, budget headroom,
97	  and recent rate-limit signals: `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json`. See
98	  "Pace yourself" below for how to act on it.
99	
100	## Your session's identity (environment variables)
101	
102	The harness exports these to every session — read them instead of guessing:
103	
104	| Variable | Meaning |
105	|---|---|
106	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT` | workspace root (use for `--root`-free CLI calls) |
107	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SKILL` | absolute path to this `SKILL.md` (never resolve it relative to the shell cwd) |
108	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` | run id (e.g. `0163`) |
109	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION` | this session's name (e.g. `0002-horizon-T-1`) |
110	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR` | this session's directory (transcript, usage.json, report) |
111	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS` | which round this is (0-based) / the run's planned total |
112	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK` / `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK_TITLE` | the task id / title (full body: `"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`) |
113	| `ARCHON_HORIZON_PROJECTS` | comma-separated projects this task spans |
114	| `HORIZON_BIN`, `HORIZON_GIT` | absolute paths to the CLI and the ledger-git wrapper |
115	| `HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR`, `HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE` | the workspace ledger repo + its work tree — `"$HORIZON_GIT" …` is shorthand for `git --git-dir "$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree "$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" …` |
116	
117	## Pace yourself (usage & interruption risk)
118	
119	Sessions end for reasons you don't control: rate limits, usage caps, budgets.
120	The defense is NOT to avoid work — it is to make interruption cheap:
121	
122	- **Commit at every coherent point** (plain git into the ledger, below). If
123	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` shows low budget headroom or recent
124	  `rate_limit`/`usage_limit` signals, commit what you have NOW and prefer
125	  finishing the piece in flight over opening a new front.
126	- If this is the run's **last round** (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` + 1 ==
127	  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUNDS`), leave the workspace hand-off-clean: commit, update
128	  the roadmap/task status, and write the report as if nobody continues today.
129	- Interrupted anyway? Nothing is lost that was committed — the next session
130	  resumes from the ledger (see "Resuming" below).
131	
132	## One-shot discipline (important)
133	
134	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
135	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**
136	(builds, checks, subagents). Anything you leave running in the background, or leave
137	uncommitted, may be lost when the session ends. Commit early and often (below).
138	
139	## Pick the highest-value work
140	
141	Read the roadmap and the live Lean state, then commit to the most valuable next
142	piece. A node being large, multi-session, or blocked on missing mathlib
143	infrastructure is **not** a reason to skip it — start it, build the missing
144	lemma/definition yourself as project-local infrastructure, and push it as far as
145	you genuinely can. Prefer ambitious progress over defensive avoidance.
146	
147	If this session was launched on a specific task, make concrete progress on that
148	task's REAL objective — don't preemptively pivot to easy unrelated wins because
149	the objective is large. Leave a `"$HORIZON_BIN" task comment <task_id> --body …`
150	at each significant step. You own the task's terminal status (skill:
151	`task-status`): set `--status done` only when the objective is FULLY complete;
152	`blocked`/`failed` if genuinely stuck; set nothing if it's only partly advanced
153	(it returns to the queue).
154	
155	## Fresh-context checkpoints
156	
157	The old Ground pass is no longer a second orchestrator role, but independent
158	review is still part of convergence. Spawn the **`ground`** subagent at these
159	checkpoints:
160	
161	- before marking a multi-step task `done`;
162	- after every two substantive Horizon sessions on a long-running task;
163	- immediately after a strategy pivot, a broad workspace edit, or a surprising
164	  clean/build result.
165	
166	Give it the task/project scope and ask it to inspect the actual ledger diff,
167	blueprint graph, Lean state, roadmap, inbox, and reports with fresh context. It
168	is read-only on source and reports issues/memory; reconcile its findings before
169	continuing. Use **`work-reviewer`** for a narrow diff/proof audit and **`janitor`**
170	when the main concern is workspace hygiene. A one-session task may skip the
171	periodic checkpoint, but must still obtain a fresh-context review before a
172	terminal `done` claim.
173	
174	Schedule upkeep even when the last command did not print a warning. On a
175	multi-session run, dispatch **`janitor` at the start of every second Horizon
176	session** and before the final report; on a one-session task, dispatch it once
177	before claiming completion if the run touched roadmap, task, or inbox state.
178	Record the checkpoint in the report and wait for the helper before continuing.
179	If `janitor` is unavailable, ask **`ground`** for the same hygiene inspection;
180	Ground is read-only, so apply or explicitly record its findings yourself.
181	
182	## Warnings are work
183	
184	Commands report problems for a reason — never scroll past them. `lake build`
185	warnings, `horizon graph sync` warnings, roadmap consistency warnings, deprecation
186	notices from any tool: if your change caused it, **fix it now** (it is part of
187	the task); if it's pre-existing or caused by the tool/command itself, don't
188	silently ignore it — record it as a memory item, file an inbox `issue`, or
189	address it `--to human` when a human decision is needed. A warning that
190	survives your session should be one you *chose* to leave, with a trace saying
191	why.
192	
193	Collection-health warnings are a dispatch trigger, not background noise. When
194	`inbox`, `roadmap`, or `task` reports an overloaded queue, stale running item,
195	or status mismatch, pause the proof loop and spawn **`janitor`** with the
196	workspace scope. Wait for it, reconcile its report, rerun the command, and
197	record any warning that remains intentionally. Do this at most once for the
198	same warning in a session; a persistent warning still needs a report or inbox
199	issue rather than repeated no-op calls.
200	
201	## Do the work (Lean)
202	
203	For any Lean edit, load `lean-check` before touching the file and follow its
204	required LSP loop: query the target with `lean_diagnostic_messages` or
205	`lean_goal` before the first edit and after each subsequent edit. Keep `lake
206	build` for the final session boundary or a specifically required kernel check;
207	LSP is enough between edits and proof obligations. Use the narrowest `lake env
208	lean` fallback when LSP is unavailable, and do not duplicate that check when the
209	configured final build covers the same files.
210	
211	**Do not `grep` for a lemma.** Grep matches names you already guessed; it cannot
212	find the lemma whose name you don't know, and that is the one that costs you an
213	afternoon. This workspace indexes every declaration in every project *and* in
214	mathlib — query it:
215	
216	| You want | Use | Not |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| "does this lemma exist, anywhere?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" search "<words or name>" --json` | `grep -r` |
219	| "what's the lemma for this *statement*?" | LSP `lean_leansearch` (natural language) | guessing names |
220	| "what matches this *type*?" | LSP `lean_loogle` (`Nat → ?a → ?a`) | `grep` |
221	| "does something in scope close this goal?" | LSP `lean_local_search` / `lean_hover_info` | reading files |
222	| "what should I prove next?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> frontier` (ranked) | scanning the blueprint |
223	| "what does this node depend on / block?" | `"$HORIZON_BIN" graph -p <project> get label:<id>` | reading imports |
224	| "is the proof right?" | `lake env lean <file>` (narrowest faithful check) | `lean_diagnostic_messages` alone |
225	
226	`"$HORIZON_BIN" search` covers **your projects and mathlib together**, which is
227	its whole point: the premise you need is usually already in mathlib under a name
228	you would never have grepped for. One query costs a second; re-proving an
229	existing lemma costs a session. If it reports a library as unindexed, fix that
230	first (`lake build`, then `"$HORIZON_BIN" search --reindex`) rather than falling
231	back to grep.
232	
233	Grep is still the right tool for what it *is* good at: finding a known string, a
234	specific file, or every call site of a name you already have.
235	
236	- Search before proving — the lemma may already exist. Skill: `leansearch`.
237	- Use the **Lean LSP MCP** for tight proof feedback, then verify with the narrowest
238	  faithful `lake` / `lake env lean` check. Skill: `lean-check`.
239	- Use the DAG to choose and scope work, not just to report it. Skill: `hgraph`.
240	- When editing blueprint material, follow the house format. Skill: `blueprint-conventions`.
241	  The blueprint is timeless mathematics, never a formalization journal. Put Lean
242	  implementation notes, failed tactics, and declaration-specific progress on the
243	  corresponding hgraph node with `graph add comment`; do not insert
244	  "Formalization note" paragraphs into blueprint `.tex` files.
245	
246	## Read the other projects
247	
248	They are in this workspace for a reason: the same lemma, pattern, or dead end has
249	often already been worked out next door. `"$HORIZON_BIN" search` spans **all**
250	projects — an existing construction in another project is a lead, whether you
251	import it, copy the approach, or read its blueprint. `references/` holds the
252	original sources (skill: `references`). Staying inside your own project because
253	the task named it is how the workspace re-derives the same thing three times.
254	
255	## Delegating beyond your team (ask permission first)
256	
257	Your normal way to parallelize is **within** your team: spawn subagents/workers
258	(skill: `subagents`) and dispatch scoped work to them in the foreground. That
259	needs no permission.
260	
261	Launching work **outside** your team — creating new tasks for other teams, or
262	spawning a whole new `horizon run` — is different: it spends the user's compute
263	and accounts, so it is **off by default**. Before you even consider it, read the
264	standing consent: `"$HORIZON_BIN" permissions --json`. It reports
265	`allow_launch_tasks`, `allow_launch_runs`, `max_parallel_sessions`, any declared
266	`accounts`, and free-form notes the user left (e.g. which account to prefer, when
267	limits reset). If both `allow_*` are false (the default), **do not** create tasks
268	or launch runs on the user's behalf — instead leave an inbox item `--to human`
269	proposing the delegation and why. Only when a flag is enabled may you act within
270	its stated caps, and follow the account/usage notes the user recorded.
271	
272	## Record progress = commit (this is how progress is read)
273	
274	Your commits — message + diff — are the durable record of what you did; the
275	dashboard reads progress from them. Commit coherent progress yourself with plain
276	`git` into the workspace ledger. Skill: `project-git` (use `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m …`
277	or the explicit `--git-dir/--work-tree` form; provenance trailers are auto-stamped).
278	
279	Write **semantic, math-first** messages that say what you proved/built. Prefer
280	staging explicit files over `add -A`. Beyond commits:
281	
282	- Update the **roadmap** with coarse status (`--status`) and strategy prose
283	  (`--summary`), not a re-narration of the diff.
284	- Use the **inbox** to hand off to the next/other sessions; record durable dead-ends
285	  as **memory**.
286	
287	Before your final report, do one boundary-maintenance pass. Re-read the task's
288	`roadmap_refs` and `inbox_refs`; update each roadmap milestone whose status or
289	strategy changed, add a concise mathematical comment for a key advance, and
290	archive or complete open inbox items your work actually resolved. Also scan the
291	remaining open inbox for consumed temporary/info/memory items and archive those
292	that are now stale. Never archive a standing protection merely to make the list
293	shorter. In particular, review every open conversation your task started: archive
294	answered threads and leave a concrete blocker on any that must stay open. This
295	pass is part of completing the work, not optional janitor follow-up.
296	
297	## Resuming after an interruption
298	
299	State lives on disk, so a fresh session (even on another account) continues
300	cheaply. Working out *whether* you're resuming, and what to read if you are, is
301	the `horizon-start` skill — load it at the start of the session. The essentials:
302	
303	- **Why did the last run stop?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json` includes a
304	  `paused` field (from `runs/<id>/paused.json`) with the reason (usage limit,
305	  budget, …) and the exact resume command; `recent_failure_reasons` shows
306	  rate-limit signals. A paused/killed run resumes with
307	  `"$HORIZON_BIN" run --resume <id>`.
308	- **What was in flight?** Read recent ledger history (`project-git` skill:
309	  `git log` + `git show` by `Archon-Session` trailer) and the previous
310	  session's transcript/report under `.archon-horizon/runs/`. A horizon session
311	  directory with **no `report.md`** is one that was killed mid-flight.
312	- **Is another run live on this workspace?** `"$HORIZON_BIN" ps` lists runs
313	  holding a process (the ledger is one shared branch — be aware of parallel
314	  writers); it also flags zombie markers and stalled runs. A run registers a
315	  `runs/<id>/process.json` marker (pid/host) at start and removes it on clean
316	  exit; `ps` decides liveness by probing the pid on the local host (a marker whose
317	  pid is dead is a reap-able zombie, a live pid idle for a long time is "stalled").
318	  The synchronizer surfaces the same "other runs live" signal at command start, so
319	  you usually don't need to call `ps` explicitly.
320	
321	## Final report (your last message)
322	
323	Your final message is saved as the session's report — a human or the next
324	session should understand the session from it without opening raw logs.
325	Recommended sections: `## Summary`, `## Progress`, `## Issues`,
326	`## Why I stopped`, `## Next` (keep at least `## Progress` and
327	`## Why I stopped`). In `## Progress`, one inline `-` bullet per file/target,
328	e.g. `- FileA.lean: 4 sorries -> 3; closed the base case.` In `## Why I
329	stopped`, say plainly whether the objective is fully complete, partly advanced,
330	or blocked — and why. Always mention build failures, broken proofs, blocked
331	dependencies, and checks that failed or were not run. If a plausible next
332	action fits in the session's scope, take it before stopping — a clean commit is
333	not by itself a reason to stop.
334	
335	## Cleaning up the work (you decide, via subagents)
336

1	---
2	name: horizon-start
3	description: Work out which situation you were launched into — first round of a fresh run, a hand-off from the horizon session that just finished, a resume after a crash or pause, or a session outside any run — and pull exactly the context that situation calls for. Load at the START of a session, before picking up the task.
4	---
5	
6	Your prompt carries the task and nothing else: no history, no word about who ran
7	before you or how they ended. That is deliberate — state is pulled, not pushed
8	(the `horizon` skill's stance). But it means a session that starts working
9	immediately is guessing. Usually somebody *was* here before you, often minutes
10	ago, and their report was written for you.
11	
12	This skill is the first pass: four cheap reads, a guess at the situation, then
13	the context that situation actually calls for. Budget a couple of minutes, not a
14	tenth of the session.
15	
16	## The four signals
17	
18	```bash
19	ls "$ARCHON_HORIZON_SESSION_DIR/.."     # sibling sessions in THIS run
20	"$HORIZON_BIN" usage --json             # `paused` (why the last run stopped) + `recent_failure_reasons`
21	"$HORIZON_BIN" ps                       # is another run live on this workspace RIGHT NOW?
22	"$HORIZON_GIT" log --oneline -15        # what actually landed recently
23	```
24	
25	The sibling listing is the one that decides most of it. A run's sessions look
26	like:
27	
28	```
29	0001-system            ← orchestrator bookkeeping (commits, integration), not an agent
30	0002-horizon-PET.5     ← a horizon session; meta.json + transcript.jsonl + usage.json
31	0003-system
32	0004-horizon-PET.5     ← ...you, probably
33	```
34	
35	For any earlier `*-horizon-*` sibling, two files answer everything:
36	
37	- **`report.md` present** → that session finished on its own terms and wrote you
38	  a hand-off. **`report.md` absent** → it was killed mid-flight. This is the
39	  single most informative bit on disk.
40	- **`meta.json`** → `round`, `task_id`, `status`, `started_at`, `ended_at`,
41	  `model`. `ended_at` against the current time tells you whether "recent" means
42	  four minutes ago or last week.
43	
44	## Which situation am I in?
45	
46	Work down the list; the first match is your best guess.
47	
48	**An earlier horizon sibling has no `report.md`** → *resume after a crash or
49	kill.* Its work is half-done and possibly half-committed. Read its commits in
50	the ledger first (they are the part that survived), then the tail of its
51	transcript to see what it was in the middle of — `usage --json` `paused` gives
52	the reason it died (usage limit, budget, auth), and `recent_failure_reasons`
53	shows rate-limit pressure that may still be there. Trust the ledger over the
54	transcript: anything it did not commit is gone, no matter what it said it was
55	doing. If the dead session shares your `ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK`, you are continuing
56	its exact work — pick up its front rather than opening a new one.
57	
58	**An earlier horizon sibling has a `report.md`** → *hand-off from the session
59	that just finished.* The common case. Read that report first — its `## Next` and
60	`## Why I stopped` were written for exactly this moment — then its commits, then
61	any inbox items addressed to horizon since its `ended_at`. Do not re-derive what
62	it already established; do not redo a piece it says is done without checking the
63	ledger.
64	
65	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is `0` and no horizon sibling exists** → *first agent
66	of the run.* Nobody handed you anything **in this run** — but the workspace is
67	almost never greenfield. Earlier runs live under `.archon-horizon/runs/`; the
68	roadmap, the inbox and the ledger carry their conclusions. Skim the roadmap and
69	recent ledger history before deciding a strategy that a previous run already
70	tried and rejected.
71	
72	**`ARCHON_HORIZON_RUN` is unset** → *not launched by the orchestrator* (an
73	interactive or hand-driven session). No run context exists to reconstruct;
74	orient from workspace state — roadmap, inbox, ledger — and say where things
75	stand before proposing work.
76	
77	One caveat about round numbers. `ARCHON_HORIZON_ROUND` is 0-based and reliable
78	for "am I first" — but a resumed run can re-run a round whose session died, so a
79	`0` with a dead sibling present means *resume*, not *fresh*. The dead-sibling
80	check settles it either way. (`ROUND + 1 == ROUNDS` is a sound last-round test,
81	resumed runs included — `ROUNDS` bounds the rounds *this* invocation drives, not
82	the run's original plan.)
83	
84	## Then, before you start
85	
86	- **`horizon ps` said another run is live?** You share one ledger branch with it.
87	  Commit in small coherent pieces and expect to see its commits interleaved.
88	- **Timestamps are context.** A predecessor that ended 90 seconds ago probably
89	  left a warm build; one that ended last week may have left a workspace that no
90	  longer compiles. Check rather than assume.
91	- **The inbox is the cross-session thread** — read what past sessions left for
92	  horizon, and the task's own comments if you share their `task_id`
93	  (`"$HORIZON_BIN" task show "$ARCHON_HORIZON_TASK" --json`). Skill:
94	  `horizon-inbox`.
95	
96	Then stop orienting and start working. The point of this pass is to begin from a
97	smarter place than round zero — not to reconstruct everything that ever happened
98	here.

The keystone of the curve substrate: for a scheme `X` proper and geometrically integral over a
field `K`, the structure map induces an isomorphism `K ≅ Γ(X, 𝒪_X)`.

* `AlgebraicGeometry.bijective_appTop_of_isProper_of_geometricallyIntegral`:
  the honest general form — `f.appTop : Γ(Spec K, ⊤) ⟶ Γ(X, ⊤)` is bijective.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.isIso_appTop_of_isProper_of_geometricallyIntegral` and the bundle instance
  `AlgebraicGeometry.isIso_hom_appTop_of_geometricallyReduced`: the instance-friendly forms.

## Proof sketch

Write `A := Γ(X, ⊤)`. By Mathlib's properness facts (`isField_of_universallyClosed`,
`finite_appTop_of_universallyClosed`), `A` is a field, finite over `K`. Base change `f` along
`Spec A ⟶ Spec K`: the total space `X_A` is again proper and geometrically integral over the
field `A`, so `Γ(X_A, ⊤)` is a field as well. Flat base change of sections
(`isIso_pushoutSection_of_isQuasiSeparated_of_flat_right`) exhibits `Γ(X_A, ⊤)` as the pushout
`A ⊗[K] A`. A pushout of a field extension along itself being a field forces `K ⟶ A` to be an
*epimorphism* of rings (`CommRingCat.epi_of_isPushout_of_isField`: the codiagonal
`A ⊗[K] A ⟶ A` is injective, being a ring map out of a field, and surjective, being split by
`inl`; hence `inl` is an isomorphism and the two coprojections agree). A finite ring
epimorphism is surjective (`RingHom.surjective_of_epi_of_finite`), and any ring map out of a
field is injective.

Geometric reducedness enters only through `GeometricallyIntegral`; for the curve bundle of the
challenge it is supplied by "smooth ⟹ geometrically reduced", proved elsewhere in this project.
-/

set_option autoImplicit false

universe u

open CategoryTheory Limits

namespace CommRingCat

/-- If a pushout square of commutative rings has isomorphic legs (`e : C ≅ B` intertwining
`ψ` and `φ`) and its pushout `D` is a field, then `φ` is an epimorphism.

This is the classical "diagonal" criterion: the codiagonal `μ : D ⟶ B` determined by
`𝟙 B` and `e.hom` is injective (a ring map out of a field into a nontrivial ring) and split
surjective, hence an isomorphism; so `inl = e.inv ≫ inr`, which makes `φ` epi. -/
lemma epi_of_isPushout_of_isField {A B C D : CommRingCat.{u}}
    {φ : A ⟶ B} {ψ : A ⟶ C} {inl : B ⟶ D} {inr : C ⟶ D}
    (H : IsPushout φ ψ inl inr) (hD : IsField D) [Nontrivial B]
    (e : C ≅ B) (he : ψ ≫ e.hom = φ) : Epi φ := by
  letI : Field D := hD.toField
  -- the codiagonal
  let μ : D ⟶ B := H.desc (𝟙 B) e.hom (by rw [Category.comp_id, he])
  have hμinl : inl ≫ μ = 𝟙 B := H.inl_desc _ _ _
  have hμinr : inr ≫ μ = e.hom := H.inr_desc _ _ _
  have : IsIso μ := by
    refine (ConcreteCategory.isIso_iff_bijective μ).mpr ⟨μ.hom.injective, fun b ↦ ⟨inl b, ?_⟩⟩
    simpa using congr($(hμinl) b)
  -- the two coprojections agree up to `e`
  have key : e.inv ≫ inr = inl := by
    rw [← cancel_mono μ, Category.assoc, hμinr, hμinl, Iso.inv_hom_id]
  refine ⟨fun {W} u v huv ↦ ?_⟩
  have w : φ ≫ u = ψ ≫ (e.hom ≫ v) := by
    rw [← Category.assoc, he]; exact huv
  calc u = inl ≫ H.desc u (e.hom ≫ v) w := (H.inl_desc _ _ _).symm
    _ = e.inv ≫ inr ≫ H.desc u (e.hom ≫ v) w := by rw [← Category.assoc, key]
    _ = e.inv ≫ e.hom ≫ v := by rw [H.inr_desc]
    _ = v := by rw [Iso.inv_hom_id_assoc]

end CommRingCat

319	variable (C : Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of k))) (κ : Type u) [Field κ] [Algebra k κ]
320	
321	/-- The first projection `C_κ ⟶ C` of the field base change is an affine
322	morphism: it is the base change of the affine `Spec κ ⟶ Spec k` (pattern
323	`isAffineHom_p1BaseChange_fst`, `Picard/RigidPushforward.lean`). -/
324	instance isAffineHom_baseChangeField_fst :
325	    IsAffineHom (pullback.fst C.hom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ)))) :=
326	  MorphismProperty.pullback_fst (P := @IsAffineHom) C.hom
327	    (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ)))
328	    (inferInstance : IsAffineHom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ))))
329

331	
332	/-- **A 2-affine Mayer–Vietoris cover square base-changes along a field
333	extension**: the preimage (`AffineCoverMVSquare.preimage`,
334	`Picard/RigidPushforward.lean`) of a bundled 2-affine cover of `C` under the
335	affine first projection `C_κ ⟶ C`. Charts are identified by
336	`baseChangeField_U₁`/`baseChangeField_U₂`. Companion of
337	`AffineCoverMVSquare.baseChangeSpecOver` (`Picard/FinitePresentationFunctor.lean`),
338	which is keyed on the `specOver k A` base shape; this one is keyed on the raw
339	`Spec.map (algebraMap k κ)` spelling. -/
340	noncomputable def AffineCoverMVSquare.baseChangeField
341	    (S : C.left.AffineCoverMVSquare) :
342	    (Scheme.baseChangeField C κ).left.AffineCoverMVSquare :=
343	  show (pullback C.hom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ)))).AffineCoverMVSquare from
344	    S.preimage (pullback.fst C.hom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ))))

347	the preimage of the first chart. -/
348	@[simp] lemma AffineCoverMVSquare.baseChangeField_U₁ (S : C.left.AffineCoverMVSquare) :
349	    (S.baseChangeField κ).U₁ =
350	      pullback.fst C.hom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ))) ⁻¹ᵁ S.U₁ :=

354	the preimage of the second chart. -/
355	@[simp] lemma AffineCoverMVSquare.baseChangeField_U₂ (S : C.left.AffineCoverMVSquare) :
356	    (S.baseChangeField κ).U₂ =
357	      pullback.fst C.hom (Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom (algebraMap k κ))) ⁻¹ᵁ S.U₂ :=

70	section Peeling

72	variable (K : Type u) [Field K] {Y : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral Y]
73	  [Y.Over (Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]
74	  [SmoothOfRelativeDimension 1 (Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K))]

81	/-- **The π-free peeling** (the abstract-witness form of DAT-0a): a single witness
82	divisor `W₀` with vanishing `H¹` makes `H¹(𝒪(D))` vanish for **every** divisor `D` of
83	degree `≥ deg W₀ + 1 − χ(𝒪_Y)` — the residual class `[D]·[W₀]⁻¹` has an effective
84	representative (`exists_effective_of_picClass`), peeling (`peel_effective`) transports
85	the vanishing to `W₀ + E`, and witness-independence
86	(`subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq`) reaches `D`. -/
87	theorem subsingleton_hModule_one_of_witness (W₀ D : Y.CurveDivisor)
88	    (hW₀ : Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K W₀) 1))
89	    (hdeg : CurveDivisor.deg K W₀ + 1 - Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K)
90	      ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K D) :
91	    Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K D) 1) := by
92	  set c : Y.CechPic :=
93	    CurveDivisor.picClass K D * (CurveDivisor.picClass K W₀)⁻¹ with hc
94	  obtain ⟨Wc, hWc⟩ := CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K c
95	  have hWcdeg : CurveDivisor.deg K Wc
96	      = CurveDivisor.deg K D - CurveDivisor.deg K W₀ := by
97	    rw [← classDeg_picClass K Wc, hWc, hc, classDeg_mul, classDeg_inv,
98	      classDeg_picClass, classDeg_picClass]
99	    ring
100	  have hWdeg : 1 ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K Wc + Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K) := by
101	    rw [hWcdeg]; linarith
102	  obtain ⟨E, hE0, hEc⟩ := exists_effective_of_picClass Wc hWdeg
103	  have hclass : CurveDivisor.picClass K (W₀ + E) = CurveDivisor.picClass K D := by
104	    rw [CurveDivisor.picClass_add, hEc, hWc, hc,
105	      mul_comm (CurveDivisor.picClass K D), ← mul_assoc, mul_inv_cancel, one_mul]
106	  exact subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq K hclass
107	    (peel_effective W₀ E hE0 hW₀)

9	# DAT-0a — the P5-uniform `H¹`-vanishing bound
10	
11	For the curve bundle `Y` (integral, smooth of relative dimension one, locally of finite type
12	and quasi-compact over a field `K`) carrying a **finite dominant** morphism `π : Y ⟶ ℙ¹`,
13	there is a single integer threshold `b`, depending only on `(Y, π)` and quantified over **all**
14	Weil divisors `D`, past which the degree-one cohomology of `𝒪(D)` vanishes:
15	
16	`AlgebraicGeometry.exists_bound_subsingleton_hModule_one_of_isFinite_toP1`:
17	`∃ b : ℤ, ∀ D, b ≤ deg D → Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(D))`.
18	
19	This is the **P5-uniform** pre-brick of the Wave-4 datum campaign (`informal/w4-datum-worksheet.md`
20	§2.1, §4 DAT-0a). It is consumed by DAT-D's uniform Grassmannian twist, where the twist exponent
21	`M` is chosen so that `deg (Θ^M) ≥ b` and the whole degree-`g` family lands in the vanishing
22	locus.
23	
24	## The route (worksheet §4 DAT-0a, collapsed form)
25	
26	The proof is the FLV-class argument (`RiemannRoch/FLVClass.lean`) with the twist specialized to the
27	fiber divisor `F = fiberWeilDivisor π` and the base twist fixed at the FLV-fiber threshold `n₁` of
28	`D₀ = 0`:
29	
30	* FLV-fiber at `D₀ = 0` (`subsingleton_hModule_divisorSheaf_one_of_isFinite_toP1`) gives `n₁` with
31	  `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n·F))` for all `n ≥ n₁`; take `n = n₁`, so the base twist `n₁·F` is fixed;
32	* `0 < deg F` (`zero_lt_deg_fiberWeilDivisor`) makes `b := n₁·deg F + 1 − χ(𝒪_Y)` a legal
33	  threshold: for `deg D ≥ b` the residual class `[D]·[F]^{-n₁}` has degree `≥ 1 − χ`, so
34	  `exists_effective_of_picClass` yields an **effective** witness `E` of that class;
35	* `n₁·F + E` is in the class of `D`; `peel_effective` transports `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n₁·F))` to
36	  `Subsingleton H¹(𝒪(n₁·F + E))`, and witness-independence
37	  (`subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq`, W6-lite) upgrades it to `𝒪(D)`.
38	
39	Because `n₁` (hence the base twist) is fixed, the effective witness carries the whole degree slack,
40	and `b` depends only on `(Y, π)` — exactly the shape DAT-D consumes.
41	-/

62	compatible with the structure morphisms, there is a single threshold `b : ℤ`, depending only on

69	threshold at `D₀ = 0`; see the module docstring for the collapsed route

71	theorem exists_bound_subsingleton_hModule_one_of_isFinite_toP1
72	    [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 0)]
73	    [Module.Finite K (Sheaf.HModule (Y.moduleKSheaf K) 1)]
74	    (π : Y ⟶ P1 K) [IsFinite π] [IsDominant π]
75	    (hπ : π ≫ P1.structureMap K = Y ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of K)) :
76	    ∃ b : ℤ, ∀ D : Y.CurveDivisor, b ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K D →
77	      Subsingleton (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K D) 1) := by
78	  obtain ⟨n₁, hn₁⟩ :=
79	    subsingleton_hModule_divisorSheaf_one_of_isFinite_toP1 π hπ (0 : Y.CurveDivisor)
80	  have hd'pos : 0 < CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) :=
81	    zero_lt_deg_fiberWeilDivisor π
82	  refine ⟨(n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) + 1
83	      - Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K), fun D hD => ?_⟩
84	  -- the residual class `[D] · [F]^{-n₁}`
85	  set c : Y.CechPic := CurveDivisor.picClass K D
86	    * (CurveDivisor.picClass K (fiberWeilDivisor π) ^ n₁)⁻¹ with hc
87	  have hcdeg : classDeg K c
88	      = CurveDivisor.deg K D - (n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) := by
89	    rw [hc, classDeg_mul, classDeg_inv, classDeg_pow, classDeg_picClass, classDeg_picClass]
90	    ring
91	  -- an effective witness of the residual class
92	  obtain ⟨W, hWc⟩ := CurveDivisor.exists_picClass_eq K c
93	  have hWdeg : 1 ≤ CurveDivisor.deg K W + Sheaf.chi (Y.moduleKSheaf K) := by
94	    have hWeq : CurveDivisor.deg K W
95	        = CurveDivisor.deg K D - (n₁ : ℤ) * CurveDivisor.deg K (fiberWeilDivisor π) := by
96	      rw [← hcdeg, ← hWc, classDeg_picClass]
97	    linarith
98	  obtain ⟨E, hEnonneg, hEc⟩ := exists_effective_of_picClass W hWdeg
99	  -- the witness divisor `n₁ • F + E` is in the class of `D`
100	  have hclass : CurveDivisor.picClass K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π + E)
101	      = CurveDivisor.picClass K D := by
102	    rw [CurveDivisor.picClass_add, picClass_nsmul, hEc, hWc, hc,
103	      mul_comm (CurveDivisor.picClass K D), ← mul_assoc, mul_inv_cancel, one_mul]
104	  -- base vanishing at `n₁ • F`, peel `E`, transport along the class
105	  have hbase : Subsingleton
106	      (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π)) 1) := by
107	    have h := hn₁ n₁ le_rfl
108	    rwa [zero_add] at h
109	  have hpeel : Subsingleton
110	      (Sheaf.HModule (Y.divisorSheaf K (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π + E)) 1) :=
111	    peel_effective (n₁ • fiberWeilDivisor π) E hEnonneg hbase
112	  exact subsingleton_hModule_one_of_picClass_eq K hclass hpeel
